citation.title: Combining List Experiment and Direct Question Estimates of Sensitive Behavior Prevalence
citation.venue: Journal of Survey Statistics and Methodology

standing_assumptions: [Setting: Section 2, p. 46 (PDF p. 4)] Suppose we have a random sample of $n$ subjects independently drawn from a large population. Let $X_i = 1$ if subject $i$ engages in a sensitive behavior and $X_i = 0$ otherwise. We attempt to measure the behavior $X_i$ using two methods: direct questioning and list experimentation. Our goal is to identify the prevalence of the sensitive behavior in the population, $\mu = \Pr[X_i = 1]$. Let $Y_i$ be the report of subject $i$ to the direct question. We assume that, under direct questioning, subjects may lie and claim that they do not engage in the behavior but will not lie and falsely claim that they do engage in the behavior. [Assumption 1: p. 46] Assumption 1 (Monotonicity). There exist three latent classes of respondents under direct questioning: those who do not engage in the behavior and report truthfully ($X_i = 0$, $Y_i = 0$), subjects who engage and report truthfully ($X_i = 1$, $Y_i = 1$), and subjects who engage but report that they do not, i.e., withhold ($X_i = 1$, $Y_i = 0$). [Direct response: p. 46] Let $p = \Pr[Y_i = 1 \mid X_i = 1]$ be the probability of a subject reporting truthfully to the direct question, given that he or she engages in the sensitive behavior. The response of subject $i$ is $Y_i = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{with probability } 1 - \mu + \mu(1 - p) \\ 1 & \text{with probability } \mu p. \end{cases}$ [p. 47 (PDF p. 5)] The probability that subject $i$ engages in the behavior, given a negative response, is therefore $\Pr[X_i = 1 \mid Y_i = 0] = \frac{(1 - p)\mu}{1 - \mu p}$. While direct questioning is sufficient to reveal $\Pr[Y_i = 1] = \mu p$, it is not sufficient to identify $\Pr[Y_i = 0 \mid X_i = 1] = 1 - p$. [List experiment: p. 47] Suppose we have a treatment $Z_i \in \{0, 1\}$. In the list experiment, treated subjects ($Z_i = 1$) receive a number of control questions and an additional question about the sensitive behavior. We denote the number of items that the subject states are applicable with $V_i$. [Assumption 2: p. 47] Assumption 2 (No Liars and No Design Effects). Reframing Imai’s (2011) formulations, we observe $V_i = W_i + X_i Z_i$, where $W_i$ is the baseline outcome (under control) for subject $i$ for the list experiment. [Assumption 3: p. 47] We further require that the treatment assignment be independent of the actual behavior, direct question, and baseline response. This is a stricter variant of Imai’s (2011) ignorability assumption. Assumption 3 (Treatment Independence). $(W_i, X_i, Y_i) \perp\!\!\!\perp Z_i$. [Assumption 4: p. 47] To ensure that all target quantities are well defined (and, later, to facilitate inference), we impose the mild regularity condition that all population variances are positive. Assumption 4 (Non-Degenerate Distributions). $\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = z, Y_i = y] > 0$, for $z, y \in \{0, 1\}$, $\mathrm{Var}[Z_i] > 0$ and $\mathrm{Var}[Y_i] > 0$. [Estimators: Section 3, p. 48 (PDF p. 6)] Define the sample means: $\bar Y = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i$, $\bar V_{1,0} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} V_i Z_i (1 - Y_i)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i (1 - Y_i)}$ and $\bar V_{0,0} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} V_i (1 - Z_i)(1 - Y_i)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (1 - Z_i)(1 - Y_i)}$. Define an estimator of $\mu$ based on (1), $\hat\mu = \bar Y + (1 - \bar Y)(\bar V_{1,0} - \bar V_{0,0})$. Let $\gamma = \Pr(Z_i = 1)$ be the probability of receiving the treatment question in the list experiment. [Standard estimator: p. 49 (PDF p. 7)] $\hat\mu_S = \bar V_1 - \bar V_0$, where $\bar V_1 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} V_i Z_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i}$ and $\bar V_0 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} V_i (1 - Z_i)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (1 - Z_i)}$. [Not printed as assumptions, but used throughout] The paper states the sampling model only as 'a random sample of $n$ subjects independently drawn from a large population'; its proofs treat $(W_i, X_i, Y_i, Z_i)$, $i = 1, \ldots, n$, as independent and identically distributed, with $Z_i$ part of the draw and $\Pr(Z_i = 1) = \gamma$ (in the application, p. 53 (PDF p. 11): 'All randomizations used Bernoulli random assignment with equal probability 0.5'). $V_i$ is a count of items on a fixed finite list and is therefore bounded; no moment condition is printed. Assumption 1 is used in the form $Y_i \le X_i$ (no subject has $X_i = 0$, $Y_i = 1$). The subgroup means are ratios, and the paper assigns them no value when a $(Z, Y)$ cell of the sample is empty (P019-E003). Printed page numbers are PDF page numbers plus 42. Appendices C to F are in the online supplement (author-appendix.pdf, 7 pp.), not in the article PDF.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Lemma 1, equation (1), and the remark after its proof
canonical_claim.location: Lemma 1: p. 47 (PDF p. 5). Proof and remark: p. 48 (PDF p. 6)
canonical_claim.statement: Lemma 1. Given Assumptions 1–4 (Monotonicity, No Liars, No Design Effects, Treatment Independence, and Non-Degenerate Distributions), the prevalence may be represented as $\mu = E[Y_i] + E[1 - Y_i]\left(E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 0] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 0]\right)$. (1) [Remark after the proof, p. 48] Note that if Assumptions 2–4 hold, but Assumption 1 (Monotonicity) does not hold, then $E[Y_i] + E[1 - Y_i]\left(E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 0] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 0]\right) > \mu$, as then $E[X_i \mid Y_i = 1] < 1$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $X_i$, $Y_i$, $Z_i$, $W_i$, $V_i$, $\mu = \Pr[X_i = 1]$ and Assumptions 1–4 as in the standing assumptions (pp. 46–47, PDF pp. 4–5). All expectations are population expectations for a single subject; Assumption 4 makes the conditioning events have positive probability.
canonical_claim.note: An exact population identity; both readers re-derived it and no finding changes it. The proof as printed (p. 48): 'Proof. By Assumptions 2 and 3, $E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0] = W_i + \mu - W_i = \mu$. (2) Then, expanding the left-hand side of (2) by marginalizing over $Y_i$, we represent the prevalence of the sensitive behavior as $\mu = E[V_i \mid Y_i = 0, Z_i = 1]E[1 - Y_i] + E[V_i \mid Y_i = 1, Z_i = 1]E[Y_i] - (E[V_i \mid Y_i = 0, Z_i = 0]E[1 - Y_i] + E[V_i \mid Y_i = 1, Z_i = 0]E[Y_i]) = (E[V_i \mid Y_i = 1, Z_i = 1] - E[V_i \mid Y_i = 1, Z_i = 0])E[Y_i] + (E[V_i \mid Y_i = 0, Z_i = 1] - E[V_i \mid Y_i = 0, Z_i = 0])E[1 - Y_i] = E[X_i \mid Y_i = 1]E[Y_i] + (E[V_i \mid Y_i = 0, Z_i = 1] - E[V_i \mid Y_i = 0, Z_i = 0])E[1 - Y_i]$. The result follows since $E[X_i \mid Y_i = 1] = 1$ by Assumption 2.' Two slips in it are corrected under P019-T11 ($E[W_i]$ for $W_i$ in (2); Assumption 1 for Assumption 2 in the last sentence). The marginalization over $Y_i$ uses $\Pr[Y_i = y \mid Z_i = z] = \Pr[Y_i = y]$, from Assumption 3. For the remark, 'Assumption 1 does not hold' means that false confessions have positive probability, $\Pr[X_i = 0, Y_i = 1] > 0$; under Assumptions 2–4 the expression then equals $\mu + \Pr[X_i = 0, Y_i = 1] = \mu + E[Y_i](1 - E[X_i \mid Y_i = 1])$ (the size of the excess is the readers' derivation and is not printed).

canonical_claim.location: p. 49 (PDF p. 7); proof in Appendix B.1, p. 63 (PDF p. 21)
canonical_claim.statement: Proposition 1. Given Assumption 4 (Non-Degenerate Distributions), the asymptotic variance of $\hat\mu$ is characterized by $\operatorname*{plim}_{n\to\infty} n\,\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu] = \frac{(1 - \mu)^2}{1 - \mu p}\,\mu p + (1 - \mu p) \times \left[\frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 0]}{\gamma} + \frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 0]}{1 - \gamma}\right]$. (3) [The hypothesis printed in the proposition is Assumption 4 only; the sentence that follows it reads 'Under Assumptions 1–4, $\hat\mu$ is root-$n$ consistent and asymptotically normal', and Assumptions 1–3 are maintained from Section 2.]
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $\hat\mu = \bar Y + (1 - \bar Y)(\bar V_{1,0} - \bar V_{0,0})$, the sample means, $\gamma = \Pr(Z_i = 1)$, $\mu$ and $p$ as in the standing assumptions (pp. 46–48, PDF pp. 4–6). $\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu]$ is the variance of $\hat\mu$ over the sampling of $n$ subjects; $\operatorname{plim}$ is applied to the deterministic sequence $n\,\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu]$, so the statement is a limit of that sequence. The paper does not define $\hat\mu$ on samples with an empty $(Z, Y)$ cell, which have positive probability for every $n$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: The printed proof (p. 63) rests on: (a) the identity $\hat\mu = 1 + (1 - \bar Y)(\bar V_{1,0} - \bar V_{0,0} - 1)$, display (8); (b) Lemma 2 (p. 48), '$\bar V_{1,0}$ and $\bar V_{0,0}$ are uncorrelated with $1 - \bar Y$', which holds conditional on both cells being non-empty (P019-T4 (b); P019-T3 (i) for the printed form); (c) the first equality of (9), the product decomposition of the variance, which is exact only in the form $\mathrm{Var}(AB \mid D) = b^2\,\mathrm{Var}(A \mid D) + E[A^2 h \mid D]$ (P019-T4 (c), (d)); (d) $E[1 - \bar Y] = 1 - \mu p$ and $\mathrm{Var}[1 - \bar Y] = \frac{\mu p(1 - \mu p)}{n}$; (e) $E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 0] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 0] = \Pr[X_i = 1 \mid Y_i = 0] = \frac{(1 - p)\mu}{1 - \mu p}$ under Assumptions 1–3, so that $E[\bar V_{1,0} - \bar V_{0,0} - 1 \mid D] = -\frac{1 - \mu}{1 - \mu p}$; (f) $\mathrm{Var}(\bar V_{z,0} \mid \mathcal{F}) = \mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = z, Y_i = 0] / N_{z0}$ on $D$. Here $N_{z0}$, $D$, $\mathcal{F}$, $A = 1 - \bar Y$, $b$, $h$ and $s_z = \mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = z, Y_i = 0]$ are as defined in P019-T4. An alternative exact route, from the validator (section 6 of the artifact): with $r = \mu p$, $q = 1 - r$, $m_z = E[V_i \mid Z_i = z, Y_i = 0]$, $\delta^* = m_1 - m_0$ and $\psi = (1 - \delta^*)(Y - r) + (1 - Y)\left[\frac{Z}{\gamma}(V - m_1) - \frac{1 - Z}{1 - \gamma}(V - m_0)\right]$, one has $E[\psi] = 0$ and $\mathrm{Var}(\psi) = (1 - \delta^*)^2 rq + q\left(\frac{s_1}{\gamma} + \frac{s_0}{1 - \gamma}\right)$, which equals the right-hand side of (3) because $1 - \delta^* = \frac{1 - \mu}{1 - \mu p}$; and on $D$, exactly, $\hat\mu - \mu = (1 - \delta^*)(\bar Y - r) + q\,e - (\bar Y - r)\,e$ with $e = (\bar V_{1,0} - m_1) - (\bar V_{0,0} - m_0)$.
canonical_claim.note: Both readers and the validator confirm formula (3) under Assumptions 1–4 (independent influence-function derivations; Monte Carlo at $n = 1000$ gives $n\,\mathrm{Var}$ of 4.10 against 4.08 from (3)). Three points a formal statement must settle. (1) Hypotheses: the proposition names only Assumption 4; this is recorded as a clarity note (P019-E002), not an error, since Assumptions 1–3 are maintained. They are needed: with $X, Y, W, Z$ mutually independent Bernoulli($\frac{1}{2}$) and $V = W + XZ$, Assumptions 2–4 hold and Assumption 1 fails, the true limit is $\frac{13}{16}$ and the right-hand side of (3) is $\frac{29}{24}$ (the batch artifact, section 'E002'). (2) Definition of $\hat\mu$ on empty cells: with any fixed bounded values there, $n\,\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu]$ converges to the right-hand side of (3) and the limit does not depend on the choice (section 6 of the artifact); without a convention the variance is undefined for every $n$. (3) The finite-sample steps of the printed proof need the corrections of P019-T4 (finding P019-E003, Minor). The sampling model is independent identically distributed draws with bounded $V_i$. In the validator's population (P019-T3) the right-hand side of (3) is $\frac{7}{6}$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Unnumbered statement after Proposition 1 (root-n consistency, asymptotic normality, the plug-in variance estimator) and Corollary 1
canonical_claim.statement: [After Proposition 1] Under Assumptions 1–4, $\hat\mu$ is root-$n$ consistent and asymptotically normal, with a consistent estimator of the variance obtained by substituting sample analogues (i.e., sample means and sample variances) for population quantities. Namely, let $n\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\mu] = \frac{(1 - \hat\mu)^2}{1 - \bar Y}\,\bar Y + (1 - \bar Y) \times \left[\frac{\hat\sigma^2(V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 0)}{\hat\gamma} + \frac{\hat\sigma^2(V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 0)}{1 - \hat\gamma}\right]$, where $\hat\sigma^2(\cdot)$ denotes the sample variance and $\hat\gamma = \sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i / n$. These properties are sufficient for construction of Wald-type confidence intervals using $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\mu]$. Corollary 1. If Assumptions 1–4 hold, then confidence intervals constructed as $\hat\mu \pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\mu]}$ will have $\mu$ $100(1 - \alpha)\%$ coverage for $\mu$ for large $n$. [As printed; the $\mu$ before $100(1 - \alpha)\%$ is a stray symbol, deleted in P019-T11 (c).] A proof follows directly from asymptotic normality and Slutsky’s theorem.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $\hat\mu$, $\bar Y$, $\bar V_{1,0}$, $\bar V_{0,0}$ as in the standing assumptions (p. 48, PDF p. 6). $\hat\sigma^2(V_i \mid Z_i = z, Y_i = 0)$ is the sample variance of $V_i$ among subjects with $Z_i = z$, $Y_i = 0$ (the deposited code uses the divisor one less than the cell count). $z_{1-\alpha/2}$ is not defined in the paper; it is the $1 - \alpha/2$ quantile of the standard normal distribution. The paper does not define 'root-$n$ consistent', 'asymptotically normal' or 'coverage ... for large $n$'; the natural reading is $\sqrt{n}(\hat\mu - \mu) \Rightarrow N(0, \sigma^2)$ with $\sigma^2$ the right-hand side of (3), $n\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\mu] \to_p \sigma^2$, and $\Pr\left(\mu \in \hat\mu \pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\mu]}\right) \to 1 - \alpha$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: (a) The plug-in identity: $1 - \hat\mu = (1 - \bar Y)\left(1 - (\bar V_{1,0} - \bar V_{0,0})\right)$, so $\frac{(1 - \hat\mu)^2}{1 - \bar Y}\,\bar Y = \bar Y(1 - \bar Y)\left(1 - (\bar V_{1,0} - \bar V_{0,0})\right)^2$ and the printed estimator is the sample analogue of $(1 - \delta^*)^2 rq + q\left(\frac{s_1}{\gamma} + \frac{s_0}{1 - \gamma}\right)$, in the notation of P019-T18. (b) The population identity $\frac{(1 - \mu)^2}{1 - \mu p}\,\mu p = \mu p(1 - \mu p)\left(\frac{1 - \mu}{1 - \mu p}\right)^2$ with $1 - \delta^* = \frac{1 - \mu}{1 - \mu p}$ under Assumptions 1–3. (c) The exact decomposition of $\hat\mu - \mu$ and the variance of the influence function $\psi$, as in P019-T18. (d) Positivity of the limit: under Assumption 4 the right-hand side of (3) is strictly positive, which the Wald interval needs.
canonical_claim.note: No proof is printed beyond 'A proof follows directly from asymptotic normality and Slutsky’s theorem', and asymptotic normality itself is asserted, not proved, in the paper. The validator's derivation (section 6 of the artifact) proves the three natural-reading statements for independent identically distributed draws with bounded $V_i$, after fixed bounded values are assigned to the subgroup means on empty cells and to the plug-in variance wherever its formula is undefined (cells with fewer than two observations, zero denominators); such samples have exponentially small probability. A formal statement needs those conventions made explicit; they are the validator's and are not printed. A reader's simulation at $n = 1000$ gives 95% Wald coverage of 0.9495. Nothing printed claims exact finite-sample coverage. The central limit theorem and Slutsky's theorem are the classical inputs.

canonical_claim.location: p. 49 (PDF p. 7); proof in Appendix B.1, pp. 64–65 (PDF pp. 22–23), ending at display (10)
canonical_claim.statement: Proposition 2. Under Assumptions 1–4 (Monotonicity, No Liars, No Design Effects, Treatment Independence, and Non-Degenerate Distributions), $\operatorname*{plim}_{n\to\infty} n\,\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu] < \operatorname*{plim}_{n\to\infty} n\,\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu_S]$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $\hat\mu$ and its limit (3) as in P019-T18. [Standard estimator: p. 49 (PDF p. 7)] Consider the standard difference-in-means-based estimator for the list experiment, $\hat\mu_S = \bar V_1 - \bar V_0$, where $\bar V_1 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} V_i Z_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i}$ and $\bar V_0 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} V_i(1 - Z_i)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(1 - Z_i)}$. [Asymptotic variance of $\hat\mu_S$, first display of the proof, p. 64 (PDF p. 22)] $\operatorname*{plim}_{n\to\infty} n\,\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu_S] = (1 - \mu p)\left[\frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 0]}{\gamma} + \frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 0]}{1 - \gamma}\right] + \mu p\left[\frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1]}{\gamma} + \frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1]}{1 - \gamma}\right] + (1 - \mu p)\left[\frac{(E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 0] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1])^2}{\gamma}\right] + (1 - \mu p)\left[\frac{(E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 0] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0])^2}{1 - \gamma}\right] + \mu p\left[\frac{(E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1])^2}{\gamma}\right] + \mu p\left[\frac{(E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0])^2}{1 - \gamma}\right]$, which is $\frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 1]}{\gamma} + \frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 0]}{1 - \gamma}$ with each arm's variance decomposed over $Y_i$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: The comparison of the two limits is an exact inequality between population quantities; the printed proof (pp. 64–65) uses: (a) the law of total variance over $Y_i$ within each arm, with $\Pr[Y_i = 1 \mid Z_i = z] = \mu p$; (b) the between-group identity that turns the four squared-deviation terms into $\mu p(1 - \mu p)\left[\frac{(E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 0] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1])^2}{\gamma}\right] + \mu p(1 - \mu p)\left[\frac{(E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 0] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1])^2}{1 - \gamma}\right]$; (c) $E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1] = E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1] + 1$ (printed with 'By Assumptions 1 and 2'; it needs Assumptions 1–3, P019-T11 (e)) and $E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 0] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 0] = \frac{(1 - p)\mu}{1 - \mu p}$, which give the third term $\mu p(1 - \mu p)\left[\frac{((\mu - 1)/(1 - \mu p) + E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 0] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1])^2}{\gamma}\right]$; (d) the first-order condition: over real $x = E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 0] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1]$, the function $\frac{(\kappa + x)^2}{\gamma} + \frac{x^2}{1 - \gamma}$ with $\kappa = \frac{\mu - 1}{1 - \mu p}$ is minimized at $x = [\gamma - 1]\kappa$ with minimum value $\kappa^2$; (e) display (10): $\operatorname{plim} n\,\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu_S] \ge (1 - \mu p)\left[\frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 0]}{\gamma} + \frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 0]}{1 - \gamma}\right] + \mu p\left[\frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1]}{\gamma} + \frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1]}{1 - \gamma}\right] + \mu p(1 - \mu p)\left(\frac{1 - \mu}{1 - \mu p}\right)^2 \ge \operatorname{plim} n\,\mathrm{Var}[\hat\mu]$; (f) strictness: 'Assumption 4 (Non-Degenerate Distributions) ensures that the inequality holds strictly', since $\mu p > 0$ and the two conditional variances given $Y_i = 1$ are positive. In closed form (the validator, section 7 of the artifact; both readers obtain the same): with $r = \mu p$, $q = 1 - r$, $\tau^2 = \mathrm{Var}[W_i \mid Y_i = 1]$, $u = E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 0]$ and $c = \frac{1 - \mu}{1 - \mu p}$, the difference of the two limits is $\frac{r\tau^2}{\gamma(1 - \gamma)} + \frac{rq\,[u + (1 - \gamma)c]^2}{\gamma(1 - \gamma)} > 0$.
canonical_claim.note: Held up for both readers; every algebraic step of the printed proof was re-derived and the gap verified symbolically and on exact cases (in the validator's population of P019-T3 the limits are $\frac{7}{6}$ and $\frac{3}{2}$, gap $\frac{1}{3}$). The asymptotic content is the two limits: that of $\hat\mu$ is Proposition 1 (P019-T18), and that of $\hat\mu_S$ is stated at the start of the proof without derivation (it is the first-order variance of a difference of two ratio means; exact finite-sample variances of both estimators are undefined without a convention for empty groups). The exact content is the strict inequality between the right-hand side of (3) and $\frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 1]}{\gamma} + \frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 0]}{1 - \gamma}$ under Assumptions 1–4. The only slip in the proof is the assumption citation in step (c), finding P019-E008 (Minor).

canonical_claim.statement: Proposition 3. Under the null hypothesis that Assumptions 1–4 (Monotonicity, No Liars, No Design Effects, and Treatment Independence) hold, $\beta = 1$. For large $n$, if Assumption 4 (Non-Degenerate Distributions) holds, then a two-sided $p$-value is given by $2\Phi\left(\frac{-|\hat\beta - 1|}{\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\beta]}}\right)$, where $\Phi(\cdot)$ is the normal CDF. [Following sentence, p. 50] A proof for Proposition 3 follows directly from calculations analogous to those for Proposition 1.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [Placebo Test I: Section 4.1, p. 50 (PDF p. 8)] Define $\beta = E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1]$. Consider estimators $\hat\beta = \bar V_{1,1} - \bar V_{0,1}$ and $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\beta] = \frac{\hat\sigma^2(V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i Y_i} + \frac{\hat\sigma^2(V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (1 - Z_i) Y_i}$. The paper does not write out $\bar V_{1,1}$ and $\bar V_{0,1}$; by analogy with $\bar V_{1,0}$ and $\bar V_{0,0}$ (p. 48) they are the sample means of $V_i$ among subjects with $(Z_i, Y_i) = (1, 1)$ and $(0, 1)$, and $\hat\sigma^2(\cdot)$ denotes the sample variance (p. 49). [Preceding text, p. 50] It is possible to jointly test the Monotonicity, No Liars, No Design Effects, and Treatment Independence assumptions. Under these assumptions, for all $t$, $\Pr[V_i = t \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1] = \Pr[V_i = (t + 1) \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1]$, thus tests of distributional equality are appropriate. ... However, since distributional equality implies that $E[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1] - E[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1] = 1$, a simple test is available. The paper does not define 'a two-sided $p$-value ... for large $n$'; the natural reading is that under the null $(\hat\beta - 1)/\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\beta]} \Rightarrow N(0, 1)$, so that the displayed quantity is asymptotically uniform on $(0, 1)$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: (a) The first sentence is exact: under Assumptions 1–3 and $\Pr[Z_i = z, Y_i = 1] > 0$ for $z = 0, 1$, $\beta = 1$ (P019-T12; as printed the hypothesis is Assumptions 1–4, which is stronger). (b) Under the same hypotheses the conditional law of $V_i$ given $Z_i = 0$, $Y_i = 1$ equals that of $V_i - 1$ given $Z_i = 1$, $Y_i = 1$ (P019-T6). (c) For the large-sample sentence: the exact ratio identity $\hat m - m = \frac{n^{-1}\sum_i I_i(V_i - m)}{n^{-1}\sum_i I_i}$ for each of the two cell means, and the influence function $\psi = \frac{Y_iZ_i}{q\gamma}(V_i - m - 1) - \frac{Y_i(1 - Z_i)}{q(1 - \gamma)}(V_i - m)$ with $q = \Pr[Y_i = 1]$ and $m = E[W_i \mid Y_i = 1]$, whose variance is $\frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 1, Y_i = 1]}{q\gamma} + \frac{\mathrm{Var}[V_i \mid Z_i = 0, Y_i = 1]}{q(1 - \gamma)}$, the limit of $n\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}[\hat\beta]$. (d) For $G$ standard normal and $0 < u < 1$, $\Pr(2\Phi(-|G|) \le u) = u$.
canonical_claim.note: Held up for both readers: $\beta = 1$ under the stated null, and the variance estimator and the two-sided $p$-value formula (with the minus sign) are as the code implements them. The range 'Assumptions 1–4' in the first sentence is a numbering misprint for 1–3 (P019-N001, Minor; corrected statement P019-T12); the printed sentence is true as it stands because its hypothesis is stronger. The paper gives no proof of the large-sample sentence beyond the analogy with Proposition 1; the influence-function expansion in (c) is the validator's (the P019-N003 artifact, section 1) and needs independent identically distributed draws, bounded $V_i$, and a convention for samples in which a $(Z, Y = 1)$ cell has fewer than two subjects. Passing the test does not establish the assumptions, as the paper says; the converse reading in the supplement is the subject of P019-T7 and P019-T8.
